EU Council wants to abolish correspondence secrecy

The EU member states want to abolish the modern secrecy of letters. In  the EU Council, the police should be able to prosecute private chat  flows and monitor such a letter communication. Experts warn that Signal  and WhatsApp could leave the EU.

The EU of citizens' rights – has this combination of words already  been heard? But the EU of governments, which is well there. The  elections in Belgium were held in parallel with the EU elections on 9.  held in June and ended with a triumph for the Flemish right-wing  conservatives (N-VA) and the Vlaams Belang. Liberal Prime Minister  Alexander De Croo immediately declared his resignation, but remains in  office. Its centre-left coalition will probably not be once again after  the losses suffered.

But now the country could end up one last coup in EU Brussels. Until  the 1. The Belgian Government holds the semi-annual Presidency of the EU  Council in July. Since the beginning of the year, the De Croo  government has been trying to enforce general chat control in the EU,  especially at end-to-end encrypted services such as WhatsApp or Signal.  EU bodies have been planning this advance for a long time. So far, there  have been one or two vetoos too much in the Council. But now France had  itself break out of the blocking minority. And so the Belgian proposal  could already be adopted in the Council on Wednesday.

The Regulation includes the title of "Rules to combat child abuse".  It is supposedly about images that record child abuse (child sexual  abuse material, CSAM), and also sent internet links should be scanned  automatically. Ultimately, it is about access to the online  communication of citizens. The laudable fight against child pornography  is the giant hammer, with which the small nail data protection and the  right to privacy for all citizens are to be sunk into the ground.
An increase in security is not expected

“Send me a Whatsapp,” you hear (still) everywhere. Many citizens use  the chat apps every day, almost self-evident, of course, also send a  picture, a meme, an Internet link. Three quarters of 16- to 74 year olds  across the EU are registered with one of the various apps such as  Skype, Telegram, Threema, etc. In Germany, 60 million alone use the  WhatsApp chat service, which has been part of the Facebook Group Meta  for some time. Since that is the case, many have been looking for  alternatives because Facebook is considered a data vacuum cleaner with  partly dubary terms of use. Now the EU wants to put it equally on the  Big Tech Group and gain insight into the private communication of the  citizens, block it or prosecute it in the event of a case. The country  bloc seizes the technical services and becomes the imitator of the large  tech companies, which it should actually include in the sense of the  freedom of its citizens.

If the EU regulation comes, app users will probably see one of these  windows at some point. In it, they are asked whether they agree to  verify their sent images, photos and videos by artificial intelligence  (AI) or not. If not, they will no longer be able to use the service or  at least not send any pictures, etc. However, it is likely that many  will agree with the new terms of use almost otherwise – and so the EU  would come a little closer to the comprehensive control of its citizens.

Those who have something to hide will simply not agree to the new  conditions and use darker channels, as they do today. So there would be  no increase in security for small children who fall victim to sexual  abuse and whose images are then spread. Ultimately, the EU regulation  amounts to suspend mass surveillance of citizens and thus possible  prosecution even where there is no plaintiff. For example, where  teenagers send lewd pictures. And AI can, of course, become erred and  possibly classify harmless content as potentially dangerous.
Legal service of the Council: Arbitrary control violates fundamental rights

Initially, even the checking of the chat messages and recorded voice  messages was planned on keywords. These are individual regulations that  were withdrawn for the first, according to the former MEP Patrick Breyer  (Pirates). In addition, France has returned a derogation for security  authorities and military, which can then continue to send pictures and  videos without these being subjected to any kind of scanning.

The Legal Service of the Council was still in force on 24. May found  that "arbitrary chat control" is still on the EU agenda for persons who  are not suspected of committing a crime and, of course, constitute a  violation of fundamental rights (in Germany Article 13 of the Basic  Law).

If the regulation comes, private chat providers can no longer keep  one of their most important promises. Signal’s president, Meredith  Whittaker, writes in a recent press release that “upload moderation” is  only a new word for mass chat control: “There is no way to implement  such proposals related to end-to-end encrypted communication without  fundamentally undermining encryption and creating a dangerous weakness  in a core infrastructure that would have a global impact far beyond  Europe.”

The claim that content is still being “checked before” its encryption  is contrary to the end-to-end principle with which WhatsApp and signal  promote itself. Signal had once developed open source technology,  WhatsApp took it over, Mark Zuckerberg has not yet touched it. According  to Whittaker, encryption and “upload moderation” do not go together –  this is an “mathematical reality” that new words could not hide either.  The EU chat control proposal is about “mass scanning” about “the same  old monitoring with a new label” using “mass scanning”.

One thing goes without saying that if the chat services were to know  about “illegal activities” due to the surveillance of image content and  Internet addresses, they would not only have to inform the EU state or  supranational authorities immediately about it, but also “act quickly to  remove or block access to access it”. The AI-supported detection of  supposedly illegal content would therefore also result in its deletion.
Whittaker: We are previously leaving the EU market

Already in May, Whittaker announced that he would rely on the EU  market rather than engage in an undermining of encryption technology.  Now Signal has remained a niche provider with 40 million users  worldwide.

In addition to the head of the Signal, the Society for Freedom Rights also protest the organisation European Digital Rights (entitled “Be scanned – or get banned!”) and the Center for Democracy & Technology (CDT) Europe strongly against the draft regulation of the Belgian Presidency.

However, even the industry giant WhatsApp recently threatened with  its retirement from India within 60 days, according to the trade  magazines Rest of World and Inside Digital.  The government had previously adopted a regulation requiring  significant services (those with more than five million users) to  disclose the first author of information. With half a billion users in  India, WhatsApp belongs to this category, similar to what is a “very  large platform” under the EU’s Digital Services Act (DSA) and is  therefore subject to EU censorship law. Due to the importance of  WhatsApp for the Indian economy, a compromise is expected.

In the EU, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Austria and Poland  have been against the plans. Now the Belgians were apparently able to  capture France through the concession for security services and the  military. The blocking minority in the Council could therefore tip this  Wednesday. It is frightening that the conditions in the EU Council have  become so scarce that a majority is tangible. Estonia, Finland, Greece,  Italy, Portugal, Sweden, Slovenia and the Czech Republic have not yet  determined.

The European Parliament in Strasbourg-Brussels spoke out in November  to maintain chat encryption. If the Council decision is taken on  Wednesday, then perhaps the hour of this Parliament could really beat:  it would then have to do everything possible to prevent chat control in  the so-called 'trilogue' of the three EU institutions.

DeFlock Lansing coalition wins vote on removing police spy cameras
September 1, 2026 1:56 PM CDT  By Peter Newman
A Flock license plate reader. | David Goldman / AP
LANSING, Mich.—“Get the Flock out of Lansing!” The chant rang through Lansing City Hall the night of Aug. 24, as more than a hundred residents packed the chambers for a city council vote that turned out to be anything but routine.

Councilmember Ryan Kost, who represents the First Ward, had introduced a resolution calling on the city administration and police department to terminate their contracts with Flock, the mass surveillance company whose 26 automated license plate readers, or ALPRs, are already installed around the city.

The cameras log every plate that passes into a nationwide, AI-powered database owned and run by Flock; the Lansing Police Department, like hundreds of others nationwide, simply pays for access.

The meeting ran more than three hours, most of that time consumed by public comment. Over 50 residents spoke against the cameras in person, and more than 30 others had emailed the council in the week beforehand. Only one speaker defended them, and he admitted he no longer even lived in Lansing. Will Lawrence, the Democratic nominee for Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, which includes Lansing, also urged the council to act.

📷Congressional candidate Will Lawrence voices his own concerns and echoes those of the community. | City of Lansing
Most of the crowd had been organized by DeFlock Lansing, a grassroots group working to rid the capital city of ALPRs. Its members wore black, held up mock Flock cameras aimed back at the dais, and closed their remarks with the refrain that gave the group its name.
Speaker after speaker raised the same fears: Officers using ALPR data to stalk former partners (one case reported elsewhere in the country involved more than 150 searches on a single person), cameras that are notoriously easy to hack, and thin evidence that the technology solves crimes at all.

Many linked the cameras to the country’s broader drift toward what they called “techno-fascism” under President Donald Trump, pressing council members—many of whom posture as anti-Trump progressives—on how they had let the cameras go up in the first place.

Public comment was capped at three minutes per speaker. LPD Chief Robert Backus faced no such limit. His lengthy remarks amounted to a string of anecdotes about cases the cameras had supposedly helped solve, paired with a contradictory claim: that Flock cameras are no different from the license plate readers Lansing has used for two decades, yet somehow far more useful than those older ones ever were.

He also insisted the cameras “do not track people” and do not feed a national database—both false, and both, if true, would undercut the very benefits he was describing. His appearance wasn’t on the published agenda; even Kost said he hadn’t known the chief would be there.

📷Councilmember Ryan Kost confronting LPD Chief Robert Backus with evidence that his own license plate data was shared with other police departments. | City of Lansing

Council questions told a very different story than Backus’s opening remarks. Kost noted that the chief had repeatedly claimed “no one is accessing our data,” then produced a 2025 FOIA response from the Pittsboro, N.C., police department stating that “Lansing, Michigan PD has a ‘relationship of access, search enabled.’”
Backus responded that Lansing had “opted out” of data sharing in 2024. Kost pressed further: A search of his own license plate through public-records requests filed around the country had turned up a hit from Johnson County, Kansas—in 2025, a full year after the supposed opt-out. Backus repeated that sharing had ended in 2024 and suggested Flock itself might be to blame; Kost said he found it hard to believe Flock wasn’t “taking a peek” at data it manages on the city’s behalf.
Backus, in turn, said he found it hard to believe a company would lie about what it had accessed, pointing to Flock’s own assurance to Kost that his plate wasn’t in its system. Trusting a non-binding denial from a surveillance company over documentary evidence apparently presented little problem for the chief.

Kost closed by saying his real concern wasn’t Lansing PD’s current policies, but rather the certainty that any policy eventually gets violated and that the risk is too serious to take that chance.

Council Vice President Trini Pehlivanoglu then asked Backus to specify exactly when data sharing had ended; he said it happened in “stages” and was “all turned off,” without saying what the stages were or naming a date. Asked whether any loophole could still let data be shared against the city’s wishes, Backus said there was none.

Councilmember Deyanira Nevarez Martinez raised the cameras’ placement, noting they sit “disproportionately in our communities of color,” and asked whether Backus thought they also disproportionately criminalized the people who live there. His answer: Cameras go where traffic is heaviest, not where any particular community lives.

“So, I want to note in those locations the primary reason they’re there is because of the size of the thoroughfare, the traffic that’s involved there, and the idea that it’s—I mean, one of these cameras in a neighborhood is not gonna provide nearly the amount, if any, benefit to us,” he said.

“It has to be on a busy roadway. That’s the number one thing.” It would appear from this answer that Backus thinks Black and brown residents live only on busy roads.

Councilmember Adam Hussain later asked him to describe the correct way to use the technology; Backus explained that an officer can “hit search one time” and see everywhere a plate has been caught on camera—which is difficult to square with his earlier claim that the system doesn’t track people.

Asked for data on how often ALPRs had actually helped the department, Backus admitted, “I’ve done a bad job in actually documenting the times we’ve used it.”

Hours after the meeting began, the council finally voted 7–1 to approve the resolution, with only Council President Peter Spadafore opposed. The chamber erupted in cheers.

The resolution is non-binding—it’s now up to Mayor Andy Schor to actually cancel the contracts—and DeFlock Lansing says it won’t stop organizing until the council passes an outright ban on ALPRs. But the size of the turnout and the lopsided vote have energized organizers, who see the win as a foundation for the fights ahead. Readers who share DeFlock Lansing’s concerns are encouraged to join the campaign.

text:
Sample letter to a Member of Parliament below should you wish to be heard. This is your right and we encourage you to use it.

Sentencing used as a political warning, not as a measure of the offence.

[Your name]
[Your address]
[Postcode]
[Email]  |  [Telephone]
[Date]
[Name of MP]

House of Commons
London SW1A 0AA

Dear [Mr / Mrs / Ms Surname],

I write as a constituent to object to the use of criminal sentencing as a political instrument. On 24 September 2026, Portsmouth Crown Court sentenced Del Somerville, 42, a father of two from Paulsgrove, to two years’ imprisonment after a guilty plea to violent disorder arising from the Eastney protest of 6 September. The court heard of a plastic bottle thrown toward a police line and swearing. The sentencing judge stated that the term was intended as a deterrent after later crowds.

Violent disorder is a serious charge. I do not ask you to pretend a bottle at officers is a joke. I ask you to notice what the bench itself said it was doing. A sentence written to frighten other citizens who might stand near a marina is no longer a measure of one man’s act. It is a message aimed at a cause. That is lawfare. It does not require a bribe. It requires a tariff set to quiet the next hundred.

In the same week, small boats reached Kent beaches without escort. In the same period, French officers have been photographed putting a knife into inflatable tubes in the surf, work this country pays toward. The bottle received two years. The landing received a review. Constituents can add. They will not be told they imagined the difference.

I reject, in all its forms, the use of an individual or a group as an example so that others will stay home. Punishment exists to fit the offence before the court. Deterrence that swallows proportion is cruelty dressed as order. It teaches the public that the statute bends with the politics of the week.

I therefore ask you, as my Member, to do the following and to write back with what you have done:

1.Write to the Lord Chancellor and Secretary of State for Justice asking whether the Sentencing Council and the Crown Court have been given any steer, circular or political expectation regarding tariffs at Channel-related protests; and if not, to say so plainly.

2.Ask for comparable tariffs: recent violent-disorder sentences where the facts were a missile at police and verbal abuse, without a Channel protest attached. Publish the comparison.

3.Raise the case, and the principle, with the Justice Committee and in writing to the Attorney General. The question is consistency, not a pardon by tweet.

4.State, on the record, that you reject sentencing designed as a warning to a lawful political constituency. One law. Like cases, like numbers.

I will remain inside the law. I expect the same of the state. I would be grateful for a substantive reply, not a party line.

Yours sincerely,
[Your name]
Constituent, [constituency]

text:
The Pothole Is Not an Accident

On the morning of Saturday, 13 June 2026, a woman named Kantha was riding her two-wheeler along the Siddapur road near Marathahalli, dropping her daughter Neha at college. It had rained heavily the night before, and the potholes had filled with water, which is the detail that makes them invisible. She hit one, lost control and fell. A school bus coming from behind ran her over. She died on the road, in front of her daughter.

A case was registered at the Whitefield traffic police station. Against the bus.

That is the whole architecture of the problem in one line. There is always a vehicle to charge. There is never a road to charge.

Kantha's death was not a freak event. In Bengaluru it is closer to a season. The National Crime Records Bureau counts deaths caused by the negligence of civic bodies, meaning bad roads, potholes, open drains, collapsing infrastructure, electrocution. Bengaluru has ranked first among Indian metros in that category for six consecutive years. Delhi, bigger and denser and not famous for good roads, recorded four in a year when Bengaluru recorded seventeen. Either Bengaluru's roads are uniquely lethal, or every other city is better at not counting.

The national picture, in passing: figures tabled in Parliament record 9,438 people killed in pothole crashes between 2020 and 2024, about five a day, the toll rising 53% across those years. The Supreme Court called such numbers frightening as far back as 2018. Yet the same table shows Andhra Pradesh, Bihar and Goa reporting zero pothole deaths in five years. Not zero potholes. Zero deaths. That is not a measurement. It is a filing decision.

A pothole death exists, legally, only if a police officer writes the word pothole into an FIR. Most do not. The crash becomes rash driving, or a hit-and-run. There is a driver to arrest and a section of the penal code that fits him. There is no section that fits an engineer who certified a road that dissolved in the first monsoon.

Bengaluru has a case that shows exactly how that works. On 6 February 2021, Tasdeeq Bushra, nineteen and in her first year of MBBS, was riding home along Hennur Main Road. She swerved to avoid a pothole. A truck hit her scooter from behind, she fell, and she went under the wheels.

The truck belonged to the Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike. The city's own civic body owned the vehicle that killed her, and the road, and the pothole she was avoiding. The driver was arrested under Section 304A, causing death by negligence. The agency was not. Her father, Mushtaq Ahmed, put it better than any court has: "We have lost our only child. Whom will we pin the blame on? The vehicle was BBMP's and so was the driver, the roads were poorly built by them." BBMP, the water board and the electricity utility then blamed one another, which is the standard procedure.

Two details from what followed are worth sitting with. The FIR did not mention the pothole. And the pothole was filled within hours of her death. The evidence was repaired faster than the case was built.

Hers is not an outlier, it is the template. The News Minute traced thirteen pothole deaths in Bengaluru between 2017 and 2022. Families compensated: zero. Officials held accountable: zero. Not for want of a policy. BBMP had notified one, three lakh rupees for a death, and reporters found zonal chief engineers who did not know it existed and had never received a claim. A right nobody is told about is not a right, it is a press release. When Ashwin, twenty-seven, died on a pothole in MS Palya, police first blamed him for riding irresponsibly. His mother fought to get one line into the FIR naming unnamed civic officers. Nothing came of it.

The courts have been trying for a decade. A petition filed in 2015 is still running, and the High Court has reprimanded the corporation repeatedly, once issuing a contempt notice after BBMP resisted paying compensation at all. At one hearing, BBMP informed the court that Bengaluru contained 221 potholes in total. The court told it to be honest.

Then came the deadline. After a student named Dhanushree was crushed by a tipper lorry in September 2025 while swerving around a pothole, the Chief Minister announced that Bengaluru would be pothole-free by the end of October, with eleven hundred crore rupees sanctioned. Officials counted potholes by the thousand and announced them filled. The deadline was missed and replaced with another. In Whitefield, residents watched gravel tipped into holes, gravel that scatters as soon as vehicles pass over it.

Here is how that pothole-free year ended. On 20 November, three weeks after the deadline, Shantamma, forty-six, riding pillion home from work, fell on a broken stretch in Hulimavu and was run over by a truck. Police blamed potholes and loose gravel. On 17 December, Tabrez, thirty-two, swerved near Nelamangala and put his front wheel into an unbarricaded pipeline pit. He died at NIMHANS two days later. Not a pothole, strictly. The same disease.

Then the rains came back in June, and so did the holes, and so did Kantha's funeral.

The exhausting part is that the effort is real. The money is spent, the holes are counted and announced, and they return on schedule, because filling a pothole is not building a road. A pothole is the visible end of a chain: a specification diluted, a layer skipped, a bill cleared, an inspection signed. Every hole in a Bengaluru road has a name attached to it somewhere. None of those names ever reaches an FIR.

A drunk driver goes to jail. A negligent engineer gets transferred. A contractor whose road failed in ten weeks bids for the next tender. The person who dies becomes a line in a table.

Bengaluru has led that table for six years and has still not produced one official who lost a job over a death. Until a road failure is something a person can be charged with, the ritual continues: a monsoon, a hole, a two-wheeler, a bus behind it, a case against the driver, gravel by the weekend, and a family being told that what happened to them was an accident.

It was not an accident. Someone built that.

National figures from MoRTH data tabled in Parliament via Outlook India (https://t.co/b0PDo3JA3g). Supreme Court 2018 via The Wire (https://t.co/AAFgu8PWf4). Tasdeeq Bushra, Ashwin and the thirteen-death investigation via The News Minute (https://t.co/tWzu3XsWhB , https://t.co/DFdBTvgXq4 , https://t.co/pgpwvlHeqC). Pest infestation to expired products: 8 restaurant licences suspended in Hyderabad

The Telangana Standards Authority for Food and Essential Drugs (TG SAFE) has suspended the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) licences of eight food establishments in Hyderabad and its outskirts following inspections that found pest infestations, expired and contaminated food, poor hygiene and storage violations, among other lapses.

The action followed a special drive by eight enforcement teams comprising food safety officers and police personnel. The teams inspected 15 establishments in the core urban region. Sixteen food samples were also lifted on suspicion of adulteration, according to a TG SAFE press note dated September 24.

Pest infestation, expired food among major violations

The eight establishments whose FSSAI licences were suspended are:

Acsys Hospitality LLP (Aroma Multicuisine Restaurant), Gachibowli : Heavy cockroach and rodent infestation, presence of cats, food infested with cockroaches and damaged by rats, expired food, labelling violations and failure to maintain pest-control and food-handler health records.

Aditya Restaurant and Bar, Safilguda : Sticky and unhygienic flooring, greasy exhausts, flies and cockroach infestation, spoiled vegetables, flaking walls and ceilings, and missing mandatory records.

Vaishnavi Darshini, Begum Bazar: Poor hygiene, fungal contamination in several food items, lack of pest-control and health records, poor personal hygiene among food handlers, inadequate lighting and improper storage of food and non-food items together.

Spicy Hub (Green Treat Restaurant), Kothapet : Greasy exhausts and walls, cockroach infestation, expired food, poorly maintained refrigerators emitting a foul smell, inadequate lighting and missing mandatory records.

Pakwan Grand Restaurant, Raidurg : Unhygienic kitchen and wet flooring, expired and wrongly labelled food, rodent infestation, cooked food stored in refrigerators, spoiled eggs and rusty, unhygienic refrigerators. Officials found 1,170 kg of expired rice bags and 45 kg of noodles with labelling defects.

Godavari Ghumaghumalu, Hafeezpet : Unhygienic kitchen and wash areas, rodent infestation, greasy chimneys, worm-infested brinjals, expired food products and missing mandatory records.

Sri Krishna Family Dhaba Pure Veg, Gopanpally : Heavy cockroach infestation, greasy exhausts, food handlers chewing gutkha and fungal contamination of food.

Sri Sai Mess Branch, Kondapur : Patchy and greasy flooring, unhygienic freezers, rotten vegetables, fly and cockroach infestation and failure to maintain mandatory records.

The inspections also found houseflies, cockroaches, rodents and rat faeces at some establishments, along with inadequate water, pest-control and health records, improper food storage and labelling, poorly maintained drainage systems and unclean utensils.

Five eateries face improvement notices

TG SAFE said improvement notices would be issued to five establishments, Girl Friend Mandi, Eat Club Brands (Box 8 and Mojo Pizza), Seasons Xprs, Yummy Bee and JMJ Boys & Girls Hostel, with reinspection planned to check compliance.

Lucky Restaurant at Pragathinagar, Bachupally, was closed for operating without an FSSAI licence, with officials also finding heavy cockroach infestation and unhygienic conditions.

A show-cause notice will be issued to Nexar Hoflich Food and Beverages (Asaa Neo Indian Kitchen) in Puppalguda, with further action proposed for penalties.

#Hyderabad #FoodSafety #TGSAFE #Telangana

An alleged error by an AI-powered traffic enforcement camera in Bengaluru has sparked discussion online after a man claimed that the system mistook his guitar for a pillion rider who was not wearing a helmet.

Souvik Dutta took to X (formerly Twitter) to share his experience, claiming that he was riding his wife's electric scooter alone while wearing a helmet and carrying a guitar strapped across his back.

According to Dutta, his wife received a traffic violation notice a few days later, imposing a Rs 500 fine for "pillion riding without helmet." The notice reportedly included an image captured by a roadside camera, which appeared to show Dutta riding alone with the guitar case strapped behind him.

Dutta shared the image and challan details on social media and tagged the Bengaluru Traffic Police, questioning the accuracy of the automated traffic-violation detection system. He also requested that the challan be cancelled.

The official Bengaluru Traffic Police account responded to Dutta's post, directing him to email automationpubbcp@ksp.gov.in for rectification of the alleged violation. The department also provided two contact numbers for assistance.

The incident subsequently drew considerable attention on social media, with users sharing their own experiences and opinions about automated traffic enforcement.

One user claimed that such errors, including alleged number-plate mismatches, were common and expressed doubts about whether the challan would be revoked.

Another commenter claimed that challenging an incorrect challan could involve prolonged follow-up and inconvenience.

A third user responded humorously to the incident, writing, "I don't see a helmet for the pillion."

The Bengaluru Traffic Police's response indicates that Dutta has been provided with a process to seek rectification. Whether the challan was subsequently cancelled or corrected was not immediately clear from the social-media exchange.

Important update. https://t.co/YBTKIgkyZP has been taken down.

After months of building this initiative for mass adoption across India (feeding it nationwide PM-to-ward-level representative data) and getting very close to public release, I received a notice from MeitY
My DNS was eventually taken down ( it's been 45 days). The concern raised was that I was using photos and information of ministers and public representatives for features such as Certificate of Shame and Leader Geotag photos.

I’m currently working through the issue with the authorities. But I also have another plan to relaunch this.

Before I reveal it, here’s what makes this project fundamentally different and why taking down a single website doesn’t actually take down the application.
I built the entire application on the Internet Computer #ICP  blockchain. The application logic and data live on-chain.

The app is still accessible through its native blockchain URL, but that URL isn’t human-friendly. So I connected it to a Web2 domain: https://t.co/ihjT4pIcBF.

The government can block the Web2 domain but they can't simply "take down" the application that exists on the blockchain.

And this highlights one of the biggest missing pieces of the decentralized web: on-chain DNS.

The ICP ecosystem is already moving in this direction, with the broader vision around DNSSEC, NNS and Chain-Key technology. ( @dominic_w @PierreSamaties
Any update on this? )

Until that becomes practical, I have two options: 1. Launch under another Web2 domain.
2. Work with an NGO/organization that can provide a more resilient layer for access, while staying within legal boundaries.

More soon.

text:
Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

Meta's notice states only that it complied with "a legal request to restrict this content". No order has been published and the legal basis, the issuing authority, and the reasons remain unknown.

We emphasise that the account is primarily engaged in acts of political speech that enjoy the full protection of Article 19(1)(a). The account has been restricted after the movement's march to Parliament over the NEET paper leak, and while the Delhi High Court examines allegations of excessive police force against protesters. Viewed in this background the blocking of its social media account at this moment is the suppression of dissent.

The secrecy compounds the illegality. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A of the IT Act on the strength of its procedural safeguards. In Anuradha Bhasin, it held that orders restricting fundamental rights must be published. These safeguards are defeated when the originator learns of a blocking action from an error message.

We also note that Meta's notice refers to a "legal request", not an order.  We call on MeitY to disclose the order, furnish a copy to the account holder, and provide a hearing. We call on Meta to inform the account holder of the specific legal process it received. Wholesale blocking of an entire account is disproportionate and unconstitutional.

text:
Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

🚨 Binance P2P se Bank Account Freeze? Poori Guide + Real Solution (2026)

Bhai aur beheno, agar aap bhi Binance P2P trading karte ho aur suddenly bank account freeze ho gaya hai toh pareshan mat ho. Yeh bahut common problem hai India mein. Innocent log bhi fas jaate hain jab kisi buyer/seller ka paisa kisi fraud case se link hota hai.

Yeh steps follow karo - 

1️⃣ Sabse Pehle Bank Branch Jaao  
   - Freeze ka exact reason, Cyber Crime complaint number, IO naam aur Police Station details lo.  
   - Written notice maang lo.

2️⃣ Saare Proofs Collect Karo (Bahut Important)  
   - Binance P2P complete order history (screenshots)  
   - Buyer/Seller ke saath chat  
   - Payment proof (UPI, bank transfer screenshot)  
   - Bank statement jisme transaction dikhe  
   - Aadhaar, PAN, Binance account details

3️⃣ Binance Support ko turant contact karo  
   - App mein Help section → Submit ticket  
   - Order ID aur proofs attach karo. Woh counterparty ko investigate kar sakte hain.

4️⃣ Cyber Cell mein Representation Daalo  
   - Local Cyber Police Station ya online portal pe jaao.  
   - Detailed application likho ki transaction genuine tha Binance P2P pe hua.  
   - Saare proofs attach karo.  
   - Lawyer (Cyber crime specialist) ki madad le lo - yeh bahut kaam aata hai.

5️⃣ Follow-up karte raho  
   - Har 7-10 din mein bank aur cyber cell ko call/email karo.  
   - Partial release ke liye request kar sakte ho.

Extra Tips jo future mein bacha sakte hain:
• P2P ke liye alag dedicated bank account use karo (savings account mat use karo)
• Sirf verified buyers/sellers ke saath trade karo
• Video verification ya proper KYC maango
• Bahut bade amounts ek baar mein mat trade karo
• Binance P2P risky hai India mein, agar ho sake toh avoid karo

is the ECI compromised?  
 In March 2026, ahead of the Kerala Assembly elections (polling on 9 April 2026), a 2019 Election Commission of India (ECI) letter redistributed by the Kerala Chief Electoral Officer’s (CEO) office was found to carry the seal of the BJP’s Kerala unit. This sparked a political row, followed by police-directed efforts to remove related social media posts

This takedown action itself became controversial, with critics framing it as an attempt to suppress discussion of an official lapse during an election period, while authorities maintained it was necessary to stop the circulation of a withdrawn and erroneous document that was being used to question the ECI’s credibility.The episode remained a flashpoint in the final stretch of the Kerala campaign, with the ECI treating it as a corrected administrative mistake and the opposition presenting it as evidence of deeper concerns about the poll body’s independence.The letter and the seal
The document was an ECI communication dated 19 March 2019 containing guidelines/FAQs on the publicity of candidates’ criminal antecedents (following a Supreme Court judgment). CPI(M) and Congress shared versions online showing the BJP Kerala unit’s seal. It had been circulated by the Kerala CEO’s office to political parties, District Election Officers, and Returning Officers as part of clarifications around mid-March 2026.thesouthfirst.comKerala CEO / ECI explanation:
It was described as a “purely clerical error.” The BJP Kerala unit had approached the CEO’s office seeking clarification on the (by then revised) 2019 guidelines and submitted a photocopy of the original directive that already bore the party’s seal. Staff overlooked this and redistributed that version. The error was identified; on 21 March a formal withdrawal notice was issued telling recipients to disregard the document. An Assistant Section Officer was suspended pending inquiry. Later, a Deputy CEO and a Section Officer were relieved of election-related duties.livemint.comOpposition parties (CPI(M) and Congress) rejected the clerical-error account. They alleged compromised institutional neutrality, claiming seals were being “casually swapped” and questioning whether the ECI and BJP shared the same “power centre.” Some BJP responses labelled the circulation of the old document as misinformation or a political plot.thewire.inDeletion of posts controversyActing on an ECI directive (under the Model Code of Conduct), the Kerala Police cyber cell issued notices to X (Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, and numerous individual accounts. They demanded removal of posts sharing the letter that carried the BJP seal.  Police argued the content insulted the Election Commission, undermined its integrity and transparency, spread false claims about a rectified clerical error, and risked public order or communal harmony by potentially fuelling political division. https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 Statement on Automated Takedown of Its Instagram Posts by Meta

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly condemns the restriction of its Instagram post discussing the censorship faced by digital fact-checking organisation Alt News, as well as the subsequent takedown of an Instagram Story in which https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 shared Scroll’s report on the matter.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 on 17th September 2026 had published a post highlighting the takedowns faced by Alt News in relation to its reporting on the Chauhaan film teaser. Alt News on 19th August 2026 had published a report on the content takedown they had faced, which was as follows. An Instagram post by Alt News based on the analysis of the teaser of the movie ‘Chauhaan’ was restricted by Instagram. A subsequent version was also removed, while a third version, after references to Hizbul Mujahideen militant “Burhan Wani” were removed, was allowed to remain online. Alt News also stated that search results for “Burhan Wani” on Instagram yielded no results and instead showed a message that said “these search terms may be associated with socially sensitive content”.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has been actively monitoring content takedowns through its Free Speech Tracker and had written extensively about the restrictions faced by Alt News and made a social media post discussing these particular instances to highlight the growing use of opaque content moderation systems on platforms and the chilling effect such systems can have on journalism and public-interest speech. The post specifically noted that such censorship can operate even without a formal government order, and that journalists may begin self-censoring if they believe that certain subjects, words or images could trigger restrictions.

Instagram subsequently restricted https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s posts in India. The notification stated that the content was restricted through “automated systems implemented under legal requirements.” The matter became even more concerning when Scroll reported on the restrictions faced by https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 and Alt News in a post on Instagram. When https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 shared Scroll’s report on the matter through an Instagram Story on its public handle, the Story was also taken down by Instagram through the use of automated systems.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 is deeply concerned about the increasing reliance on automated systems for implementing content restrictions and legal compliance requirements. The lack of clarity around this notification further adds to the concern. Since the content has been taken down by automated systems it is unclear whether the restriction stems from a specific legal request or order issued to Meta, or whether Meta has restricted the content suo motu through its automated systems as part of its compliance with the due diligence requirements under the Information Technology Rules, 2021. https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has not been provided with sufficient information to determine the source of the restriction, the specific legal basis for it, or the process through which the decision can be challenged.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 emphasises that journalists and news outlets are facing systemic suppression due to over-automated content moderation systems that lack context for investigative reporting, public interest documentation, and critical commentary. By conflating legitimate reporting on sensitive or controversial issues with violations of Community Standards or legal requirements through automated moderation, Meta effectively silences public-interest journalism without human oversight. This opaque suppression undermines press freedom, as well as the public’s right to reliable information, and leaves users without timely recourse to contest improper takedowns.

This situation is exacerbated by the fact that the official Grievance Officer intake form for reporting does not provide a method to report the takedown of content, either for violations of Meta Community Standards, Terms of Service, or through “automated systems implemented under legal requirements”. The response from the Meta AI support assistant instead asks users to physically send an email to the resident Grievance Officer, creating an entirely separate standard for reporting content takedown as opposed to other grievances. As per the Meta platforms the email available on the website can only be used to enquire about the grievance redressal mechanism and not to file a Grievance Office report. This not only creates excessive additional friction for users, but in the case of news reporting, effectively silences journalists and curbs the spread of information for significant periods of time. This also creates a structural barrier to access further remedies such as approaching the Grievance Appellate Committee, which mandatorily requires a Grievance Officer report to be filed prior to filing an appeal.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls upon Meta to restore https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s post with immediate effect and provide a clear explanation of the legal basis for the takedown. Meta must also ensure meaningful human oversight for restrictions and provide users with an effective and timely mechanism to challenge erroneous takedown especially if done by automated systems. https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 further calls upon the Government to provide greater transparency about the legal and policy basis for content restrictions and to clarify whether restrictions were imposed pursuant to government or law-enforcement requests or through Meta’s own systems. The Government should also ensure that the users are provided with meaningful, accessible and timely avenues to contest takedowns.

The Special Intensive Revision is not only about checking electoral rolls. It is also a large-scale exercise in collecting, digitising and matching personal data. When the system cannot match an elector to an old database, the burden shifts back to the individual to prove their identity, eligibility and place on the roll. (1/10)

Read more: https://t.co/2iX4uT7GnX

This creates a basic administrative question. If an elector is already on the roll, and the state’s own database or digitisation process fails to establish a match, why should the consequences of that failure fall primarily on the elector? The answer cannot simply be another form or another document. The process must account for errors in the data, the software and the administration itself. (9/10)

The SIR ultimately depends on a chain of databases, forms, photographs, mobile numbers, family linkages, legacy records and software-generated classifications. Each link can introduce an error, but the final burden is often placed on the individual whose record has been flagged. A meaningful verification process therefore requires more than notice and hearing. It requires transparency about what data is collected, how it is matched, how long it is retained, how errors are corrected and why different categories of electors appear to receive different treatment. (10/10)

text:
The software deciding who gets on India's electoral roll is a black box. ERONET was built by C-DAC, quietly handed to TCS, and the Election Commission hasn't said a word about audits, versions or updates. Even judges, ex-ministers and veterans are getting SIR notices.

We're digging in with explainers, RTIs and questions to every body involved.

The Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls is being litigated as a question of the Election Commission’s powers. But behind the notices sent to millions of electors is another question that has received far less scrutiny, what software is deciding who gets flagged, on what data, and according to which rules? (1/10)
Read our full analysis: https://t.co/rvvpP20PlY

That question has now reached the Supreme Court. On 22 September, while hearing a challenge to the Delhi SIR, the Court questioned whether notices appeared to have been issued “almost mechanically” and asked the ECI to clarify the meaning of “logical discrepancy”. The Court also sought clearer guidance on what documents could resolve particular discrepancies and directed that responses should be possible through WhatsApp or email without insisting on physical appearance. (9/10)

The legal safeguards recognised by the Supreme Court require notice, an opportunity to be heard, a reasoned decision and an appeal. Those safeguards cannot operate meaningfully if the person receiving a notice does not know what rule triggered it, what data was relied upon or what evidence would address the alleged discrepancy. SIR is ultimately about electoral rights, but it is also about the software through which those rights are administered. The ECI should publish the systems, rules, audit records and operational protocols governing this process. (10/10)
